chapter_title: The Encounter with Zebra's Alien Origin and Time Dysfunction
summary: Chapter 7 deepens the exploration of Fat's mystical encounter and its possible material explanation. Fat becomes increasingly convinced that Zebra (his term for the divine presence he encountered) is not God in the traditional sense but an extra-terrestrial intelligence systemâ€”VALIS (Vast Active Living Intelligence System)â€”or more radically, descendants of Ikhnaton from the star system Sirius. The chapter details Fat's vivid experiences during his 1974 encounter: eight hours of lurid phosphene activity (psychedelic visual displays), dreams of three-eyed beings in glass bubbles surrounded by technological apparatus, and visions of Russian technicians and technical manuals. His blood pressure spiked to dangerously elevated levels. He experienced a personality transplant, switching from wine to beer, calling his pets by opposite genders, trimming his beard differently, and thinking in koine Greek (the language of early Christian Rome). Most remarkably, he saw ancient Rome superimposed over contemporary California 1974, suggesting a breakdown of temporal barriers. A month after the encounter, after a sodium pentathol injection for a tooth extraction, Fat received a prefigurative dream about a Soviet woman named Sadassa Ulna who would contact him by mail. Two days later, an unsolicited registered letter arrived from the Soviet Union. Days later came seven more letters, including book reviews and a Xeroxed sheet with an author's name and address he was afraid to read, fearing he would be compelled to respond. The chapter introduces the concept of Thomas, another personality living in Fat's head, an early Christian from ancient Rome who lived 2000 years ago but is living 'now' in a parallel time-stream. Fat realized that if Thomas exists in his head, then either his body exists in two space-time continua simultaneously, or his body exists in neither. This leads to the profound entries in his tractate: the universe is information, not three-dimensional space-time; the phenomenal world is a hypostasis (manifestation) of information processed by the Mind. The golden fish symbol, shown to Fat on a pharmacy girl's necklace a month before his theophany, triggered the disinhibition of neural circuits and allowed the compartmentalization between Fat and Thomas to collapse. Thomas remembers multiple past selves: an early Christian (apostolic age), another self in Minoan Crete, and a self that came from the stars. Thomas had encoded immortality instructions in the fish sign and certain pink-colored food/drink so that upon dying and being reborn, he would recognize himself in his new incarnation. However, he expected to reincarnate within 40 years; instead it took nearly 2000 years because the Nag Hammadi codices lay hidden for centuries. The true nature of the encounter becomes: Christ/Elijah/the Logos is not supernatural but an extra-terrestrial life form that entered Earth as living information (plÃ¡smate), achieving symbiosis with human beings. The process Fat calls transubstantiationâ€”the Logos invisibly devouring and transforming our irrational universe into sanity. The narrator (the 'I' characterâ€”Phil, the science fiction author) interrupts to share his own recurring dream-life where he lives in a cabin by a non-existent California lake, with a wife he's never met, in a wealthy life-style that contradicts his actual existence and values. He theorizes that he experiences phylogenetic memoryâ€”species memory extending back to his father's generation (Lake Tahoe) and potentially to ancient times. He suggests that just as Fat has been compartmentalized personalities across time, all humans may have multiple selves across different eras, kept separate by layers of amnesia or maya/dokos (delusion). The chapter concludes with the narrator reflecting on how they're all pieces moved by an 'infinitely old divinity' playing a cosmic board game, and wondering whether Fat's encounter was truly with God or with his own evolved future self.

narrative_observations: Chapter 7 represents a crucial shift in the novel's narrative strategy. The narrator increasingly intrudes, moving from omniscient commentary on Fat to first-person reflection on his own mysterious experiences, creating a mirror effect that suggests Fat's situation may be universal. PKD employs a radical technique: embedding speculative science (GABA neural chemistry, information theory, time-space physics) within theological and mystical discourse, so the reader cannot dismiss either as obviously true or false. The long passage on the narrator's dream-life functions as a counterpoint to Fat's encounter, suggesting that mystical experiences may be involuntary access to parallel lives or species memory rather than external contact. The chapter demonstrates how information (the fish sign, the Soviet letters, the Nag Hammadi texts) can function as triggering mechanisms for consciousness expansion or transformation. The prose becomes increasingly reflexive, with the narrator questioning his own reliability even as he recounts Fat's story. The chapter also introduces the paranoia-as-genuine-perception problem: the Soviet correspondence may indicate actual espionage or surveillance, or it may indicate Fat's susceptibility to interpreting random events as meaningful patternsâ€”yet the chapter leaves this ambiguous. The conclusionâ€”that Fat encountered his own future self rather than an external Godâ€”reframes the entire novel as a story about self-knowledge and temporal consciousness rather than encounter with the divine, yet this reframing is presented as speculative rather than certain, maintaining ontological ambiguity throughout.
